item.title: What is a life coach? A plain-English guide to what coaches do
item.description: What is a life coach? A plain-English guide to what coaches actually do, what they don't do, what they cost, and how to tell if coaching is what you need.
item.content:encoded:
"What is a life coach, anyway?"

Fair question. The title gets used for everything from career strategy to crystal readings. Your cousin's friend is one. Your old boss is one now. Somebody on Instagram is one with a ring light and a waitlist.

So here's the plain version, with no sales pitch hiding in it.

What is a life coach, in simple terms?

A life coach is someone who helps you get from where you are to where you want to be. They help you get clear on what you want, notice what's in the way, make a plan, and actually follow through.

Coaching looks forward. It's less "why am I like this?" and more "okay, so what now?"

A good coach listens hard, asks the question you've been avoiding, and won't let you off the hook when you say "I'll start Monday" for the ninth Monday in a row.

What does a life coach help with?

People hire coaches for all kinds of things:

  • A career change, or figuring out whether to make one
  • Starting or growing a business
  • Getting control of their time
  • Changing their relationship with money (the feelings, not the investments)
  • A big decision they keep circling
  • Rebuilding after a divorce, a move, an empty nest or a loss
  • Feeling like they've lost themselves in everyone else's needs

The common thread: you want something to change, and you want help making it happen.

What doesn't a life coach do?

This part matters, so let's be clear.

A life coach is not a therapist. Coaches don't diagnose, and they don't treat depression, anxiety disorders, trauma or addiction. If something is affecting your health or your ability to get through the day, a licensed therapist or your doctor is the right call.

A life coach is not a financial advisor. A coach can help with the feelings and habits around money. Investment, tax and debt decisions belong with a qualified financial professional.

A life coach is not a crisis line, and neither are we. (Crisis help is at the end of this post.)

If you want the full side-by-side, read therapist vs life coach vs emotional support.

Do life coaches need a license?

In the US, "life coach" isn't a licensed title. That means anyone can use it. Some coaches have serious training and years of experience. Some took a weekend course. Some have neither.

That's not a reason to avoid coaching. It's a reason to ask good questions before you hire someone: What's your training? What happens in a session? How do I leave if it isn't working? What do you do if I need more help than coaching?

A good coach will be glad you asked.

How much does a life coach cost?

Prices vary a lot. Industry guides put most coaches in these ranges (Noomii):

  • Newer coaches: about $75 to $150 a session
  • Experienced coaches: about $150 to $300 an hour
  • Specialized coaches: $300 to $500
  • Three-month packages: often a few thousand dollars

For more on what you get at each price, see how much does a life coach cost.

Is a life coach the same as emotional support?

Not quite, and this is where a lot of people spend money they didn't need to.

Coaching is built for change over months. Emotional support is built for right now. Sometimes you don't need a twelve-week plan. You need one calm human to listen for half an hour while you say the thing out loud, so your body can settle down and your brain can come back online.

Both are good. They're just different jobs.

Try this: the "what kind of help" check

Grab a pen and answer these three questions honestly:

  1. Is there a specific thing I want to change in the next 6 to 12 months? If yes, that's coaching territory.
  2. Do I mostly need to be heard this week? If yes, start with emotional support.
  3. Is this affecting my sleep, my health, or my ability to function for weeks now? If yes, please start with your doctor or a licensed therapist.

You might answer yes to more than one. That's normal. Start with whichever feels most urgent.

So do I need a life coach?

Maybe. Coaching is great when you're ready to work on a goal and you want someone in your corner who won't let you slide.

If you're not sure what you need yet, take the 2-minute "What do I need right now?" quiz. You'll get a plain answer and one thing to try today.

And if you already know you want deep, year-long work on your time, your money and your Soul, take a look at Year of YES! Coaching with Tracee Sioux. It's by application, so you'll both know it's a fit before you start.

Not a crisis line. If you're in danger or thinking about suicide, call or text 988 (US).

item.title: What is earthing? A gentle, no-hype guide to grounding outside
item.description: Earthing, or grounding, means spending time with your bare skin touching the earth. Here's what it is, why people love it, and how to try it without the hype.
item.content:encoded:
If you've heard people talk about "earthing" or "grounding," you might picture someone barefoot in a field, eyes closed, looking very peaceful. That's not far off.

Earthing simply means spending time with your bare skin in contact with the ground: grass, soil, sand or stone. That's it. No equipment, no cost, no special skills.

Here's a plain guide to what it is, why so many people are drawn to it, and how to start.

What earthing actually is

Earthing is the practice of physically connecting with the earth's surface. Most often that means walking or standing barefoot outside, but it can also mean sitting on the grass, putting your hands in garden soil or lying on the beach.

Some researchers have studied possible effects on the body. That research is still early and small, so we won't make promises about what it does. What we can say is simpler: many people find that time barefoot outside helps them feel calmer, more present and more connected to the day.

Why it feels good

Even if you set the science aside, there are good reasons earthing feels nourishing:

  • You slow down. You can't rush barefoot over gravel. You have to pay attention.
  • You come back to your senses. The cool grass, the texture of sand and the warmth of a sunny rock pull your attention out of your head and into your body.
  • You're outside. Fresh air, daylight, sky. Most of us don't get enough of any of them.
  • It's a pause. For five or ten minutes, nobody needs anything from you.

How to start, even in winter

You don't need a meadow. Start where you are.

  1. Find a natural surface. Grass, dirt, sand or unsealed stone. Concrete sidewalks and wooden decks don't count in the traditional sense, but stepping outside still helps.
  2. Take off your shoes. If it's cold, start with two minutes. Your feet will tell you when it's enough.
  3. Stand or sit still. Notice the temperature, the texture, your breath.
  4. Add a little time each day. Five minutes is a great habit. Twenty is a treat.
  5. Pair it with something you already do. Your morning coffee, a phone call or watching the kids play.

Cold-weather options: put your hands in a pot of soil, stand on a patch of lawn for one minute, or save longer sessions for sunny afternoons. Safety first: skip it on ice, sharp ground or anywhere that isn't clean.

Make it a habit you actually keep

The hardest part of earthing isn't doing it. It's remembering. That's why we built Earth Charge into the Nest app: a simple timer for earthing and morning sun, a streak to keep you going, and a daily tally of your outdoor time, all kept on your own phone.

Or start simpler: grab our free Earthing Starter Checklist, a one-page guide with a 14-day tracker you can stick on the fridge.

Earthing won't solve your problems. But five quiet minutes with your feet on the ground is a kind thing to give yourself, and kindness adds up.

item.title: How to get unstuck: 5 questions that get you moving again
item.description: Wondering how to get unstuck at work or in life? These 5 honest questions help you find what's really in the way and one next step you can take today.
item.content:encoded:
"How do I get unstuck?"

Maybe you typed it at 11 pm. Maybe you typed it at your desk between two meetings, staring at the same project you've been "about to start" for three weeks. Either way, you're not lazy and you're not broken. You're stuck. That's a real state, and there's a way out of it.

Here's the thing most advice gets wrong: it hands you a plan before it finds out why you're stuck. A new planner won't help if the problem is fear. A pep talk won't help if the problem is that you're exhausted. So before you do anything, ask better questions.

Why do I keep getting stuck?

Stuck isn't one thing. It's a symptom. Underneath it there's usually one of a few causes: you don't know the next step, the next step brings up a feeling you'd rather not have, you have nothing left in the tank, or you're chasing something that isn't really yours. (We go through the common ones in feeling stuck in life.)

The fix depends on the cause. That's why questions come first.

What questions help you get unstuck?

Grab a notebook or a notes app. Give yourself ten minutes. Answer these honestly, not impressively. Nobody is grading this.

1. What exactly am I stuck on? Name it in one sentence. Not "my career." Something like "I haven't updated my resume" or "I keep avoiding the budget meeting." Vague problems can't be solved. Specific ones can.

2. What's the very next physical action? Not the goal. The action. "Open the document." "Email Jen." "Block 30 minutes on Thursday." If you can't name the next action, you've found your problem: you're missing information, and your next step is to go get it.

3. What am I afraid will happen if I do it? This is the one people skip. Maybe you're afraid it won't be good enough. Maybe you're afraid someone will be disappointed, or that you'll find out the thing you wanted isn't possible. Write it down. Fears look smaller on paper than they do in your chest.

4. Do I actually have the energy for this right now? Be honest. If you're running on four hours of sleep, back-to-back meetings and a household that depends on you, the answer might be no. That's not a character flaw. It's capacity. When capacity is the issue, the next step isn't "push harder." It's "settle first." The 10-Minute Human Reset is a good place to start.

5. Whose want is this? Sometimes we're stuck because some part of us doesn't actually want the thing. It's the promotion your parents would brag about, or the goal you set five years ago when you were a different person. If the honest answer is "not mine," you're not stuck. You're being told something.

What do I do with my answers?

Look at what you wrote. One question probably hit harder than the others. That's your clue.

  • If question 2 was hard, your problem is information. Break the task down until the first step takes ten minutes or less.
  • If question 3 was hard, your problem is emotion. Say the fear out loud to someone you trust. A lot of stuck melts once the scary part has been said to another human.
  • If question 4 was hard, your problem is capacity. Drop, delegate or shrink one thing this week before you add anything.
  • If question 5 was hard, your problem is direction. Give yourself permission to want something different.

Then take one step. Just one. Movement creates clarity. You don't have to know the whole path to take the next step on it.

Can talking it through actually help?

Yes, and it's one of the fastest routes out. When you think alone, you go in circles. When you say it out loud to someone calm, you hear yourself. You notice the part you've been skipping. Your body settles a little, and a settled body thinks more clearly than a stressed one.

If you don't have someone like that right now, that's exactly what our 30-minute support calls are for. One issue, one real person, one clear next step. Not therapy, not coaching, just a calm human helping you think out loud.

Your next step

Not sure which kind of stuck you are? Take the 2-minute quiz, "What do I need right now?". You'll get a plain answer and one thing to try today.

And if stuck has turned into something heavier, like feeling hopeless for weeks or not being able to get out of bed, please talk to your doctor or a licensed therapist. You deserve that care. Not a crisis line. If you're in danger or thinking about suicide, call or text 988 (US).

item.title: I don't need therapy, I just need someone to talk to: your options
item.description: Sometimes you don't need a long-term plan. You just need a calm, neutral person to help you think. Here are your options, and how to choose.
item.content:encoded:
"I don't need therapy. I just need someone to talk to."

It's a common feeling. And it makes sense. Not every hard week needs a long-term plan, an intake form or a waiting list. Sometimes you just need to say the thing out loud to someone calm and neutral, and hear yourself think.

Here's how to find that kind of support, and how to make the most of it.

Why talking to a neutral person is different

Friends and family love you, which is exactly why they're not always the easiest people to talk to. They have opinions. They worry. They take sides. Sometimes they're part of the situation.

A neutral listener has no stake in your decision. They aren't hurt if you vent about your family. They don't need you to be okay so they can relax. That freedom makes it easier to be honest, and honesty is usually where clarity starts.

Your options for "just talking"

A trusted friend, with a clear ask. Friends are often happy to help when they know what you need. Try: "I don't need advice. Can I just talk for ten minutes?"

A support call. At The Emotional Support Line, you can book a 30-minute call with a trained supporter. It's one issue, one real person and one clear next step. You don't need a membership, and there's no sales call first. It's emotional support, not therapy: we listen, reflect back what we hear and help you find your footing.

A coach. If you want to change something over months rather than get through one hard week, coaching can help you set direction and stay accountable.

A peer group. Being around people who understand can be a relief. Look for groups tied to what you're going through, such as caregiving, parenting or a life change.

A licensed professional, when it's more than a hard week. If you're dealing with something long-term, or what you're feeling is affecting your sleep, work or safety, a licensed mental health professional is the right kind of help. There's no shame in it.

How to get the most out of a conversation

  • Pick one thing. "Everything" is too big to work through in one go. Choose the one issue weighing on you most.
  • Say what you want from the conversation. Do you want to vent, untangle a decision or plan a hard conversation?
  • Notice what you say twice. The thing you keep coming back to is usually the thing that matters.
  • End with one small step. Not a life overhaul. One thing you'll do in the next 24 hours.

What a support call is like

You pay, pick a time and we call you. We'll ask what's on your mind, listen without judgment and reflect back what we hear. We'll ask questions that fit how you make decisions. The goal is that you hang up feeling a little lighter and clearer about what to do next.

You don't have to have the right words. You don't have to be in crisis. You just have to want to feel a little less alone with it.

If you're thinking about suicide or you're in danger, please call or text 988 (US) or call 911. We're not a crisis line, and they're trained to help right away.

item.title: Dysregulated nervous system? 9 everyday signs and what helps
item.description: Think you have a dysregulated nervous system? Here are nine everyday signs, what's going on underneath, and three simple ways to settle your body today.
item.content:encoded:
"Is my nervous system dysregulated, or am I just bad at life?"

If you typed something like that into a search bar at 11 pm, welcome. You're not bad at life. And you're in good company.

"Dysregulated nervous system" has become a popular phrase, and for good reason. It gives a name to something a lot of us feel and can't explain: a body that's stuck on high alert, or stuck on off, long after the stressful thing is over.

Let's make it plain.

What does a dysregulated nervous system actually mean?

Your nervous system is always scanning for safety. When it senses a threat, it revs you up (fight or flight) or shuts you down (freeze). When the threat passes, it's supposed to settle back to calm.

"Dysregulated" is everyday shorthand for: the settling part isn't happening easily. You stay revved, or you stay shut down, or you swing between the two.

It's not a diagnosis. It's a description. And it's something nearly everyone goes through at some point, especially during long stretches of stress, caregiving, grief, money worries or plain old Busyness.

What are the signs of a dysregulated nervous system?

Here are nine common ones. You don't need all of them. Most people recognize three or four.

  1. You startle easily. A door closes and your whole body jumps.
  2. Small things feel huge. A spilled drink or a vague email ruins the afternoon.
  3. You can't sit still, or you can't get up. Restless and wired, or heavy and flat. Sometimes both in one day.
  4. Your sleep is off. Tired all day, wide awake at night, mind running laps.
  5. You snap, then feel awful. Your fuse is short and you know it.
  6. You can't focus. You read the same paragraph four times.
  7. You go numb. You scroll for an hour and couldn't tell anyone what you saw.
  8. Your body is holding it. Tight jaw, high shoulders, shallow breath, stomach in knots.
  9. Rest doesn't feel restful. You finally sit down and your brain says, "Now let's review every mistake you've ever made."

Recognize yourself? That's useful information, not a verdict. A body that's on high alert is a body that's been working hard to protect you.

Why does my nervous system feel stuck?

Usually because it hasn't had enough signals of safety lately. Some common reasons:

  • Stress that never really ends (a job, a sick parent, a messy household).
  • Doing everything alone, with no one to lean on.
  • Not enough sleep, food, daylight or time outside.
  • Old patterns that taught your body to stay on guard.

The fix isn't to try harder. It's to give your body more evidence that, right now, in this moment, you're okay.

How do I calm a dysregulated nervous system?

Here's a short practice you can do right now, wherever you are. It takes about three minutes.

The Settle-Down Three

  1. Name it. Say quietly, "I'm on high alert right now." Naming a feeling often takes a little of its heat away.
  2. Breathe out longer than you breathe in. In for a count of four, out for a count of six or eight. Do five rounds. The long exhale is the important part.
  3. Look around and find five things. Let your eyes move slowly around the room. Name five things you can see. This tells your body you've checked, and nothing is chasing you.

Then feel your feet on the floor for a few seconds. That's it.

It won't fix your whole life. It will often take the edge off enough to make the next decision with a clearer head. If you want the full version, the free 10-Minute Human Reset walks you through it step by step.

Can I regulate my nervous system on my own?

Partly, yes. Breathing, movement, sunlight, time outside and sleep all help.

But here's the part a lot of self-help skips: humans are built to calm down with other humans. A steady voice on the other end of the line can settle you faster than an hour of trying alone. That's called co-regulation, and we wrote a whole guide on it: what is co-regulation?

If you don't have a calm person in your life to lean on right now, that's not a personal failing. It's just a gap. And gaps can be filled.

When is it more than a dysregulated nervous system?

If you've felt hopeless, unable to function, or unable to enjoy almost anything for weeks, please talk to your doctor or a licensed therapist. That deserves real care, and you deserve to get it. Therapy is the right place for diagnosis, trauma treatment and ongoing conditions.

We're not a crisis line. If you're in danger or thinking about suicide, call or text 988 (US).

What's my next step?

Not sure if you need to calm down, talk it through, or take action? Take our free 2-minute quiz, "What do I need right now?". Six questions, a plain answer, and one thing to try today.

And if what you need is a real, calm human for 30 minutes, we're here for that too.

item.title: Not in crisis, but not okay: what to do in the in-between
item.description: When you're not in danger but you're not fine either, it's easy to feel like your struggle doesn't "count." It does. Here's what helps in the in-between.
item.content:encoded:
There's a strange, lonely place a lot of people live in. You're not in danger. You're getting up, going to work, feeding people, answering texts. From the outside, you're fine.

But you're not okay either.

Maybe your chest is tight most of the day. Maybe you cry in the car. Maybe you've stopped looking forward to anything. And because nothing is technically "wrong," you tell yourself you don't have the right to ask for help.

This post is for the in-between.

Your struggle counts, even if it isn't an emergency

We tend to think help is only for big moments: a crisis, a health scare, a loss everyone can see. So we wait. We wait until it gets worse, as if we need to earn support by falling apart completely.

You don't have to wait. Feeling heavy, stuck or quietly overwhelmed is a real reason to reach out. Small problems that get attention early tend to stay smaller.

Signs you're in the in-between

You might recognize a few of these:

  • You feel flat, tired or on edge most days, and you can't say exactly why
  • You keep saying "I'm fine" and hearing how hollow it sounds
  • Little things make you snap or cry
  • You've stopped calling friends because you don't want to be "a downer"
  • You lie awake replaying the same conversation or worry
  • You're carrying something you haven't said out loud to anyone

None of this means something is wrong with you. It means you're human, and you've been carrying a lot.

What helps, starting today

Say it out loud to one person. Not a full confession. Just one honest sentence: "I've been having a really hard time lately." Many people find that naming a feeling to a calm listener takes some of its weight away.

Lower the bar for the day. In the in-between, ordinary tasks cost more energy. Pick the three things that truly must happen today and let the rest wait.

Get outside for ten minutes. Step outside, look at the sky, put your feet on grass if you can. It won't fix everything. It's a small reset that asks very little of you.

Write down what's actually on your mind. Worries feel bigger when they're spinning in your head. On paper, they become a list you can look at.

Notice what's yours to carry. A lot of heaviness comes from holding other people's feelings and problems. Ask yourself: what part of this is actually mine?

When to talk to someone

If you've been feeling this way for a while, it can help to talk it through with someone outside your life. That means someone who isn't your partner, your mother or your best friend. Someone neutral, who can listen without needing anything back.

That's exactly what our support calls are for. They're 30 minutes with a real, trained person (never AI), focused on one thing that's weighing on you, so you leave a little steadier and clearer about your next step.

If it ever becomes more than the in-between

If you start thinking about ending your life, or you feel you might hurt yourself or someone else, that's no longer the in-between. Please call or text 988 in the US (the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline), or call 911. They're trained for exactly this, any hour of the day.

For everything short of that, you're allowed to ask for help now. You don't have to wait until it's worse.

item.title: Talk to someone without starting therapy (or touching insurance)
item.description: Want to talk to someone, but not start therapy, file insurance or use your employer's plan? Here's what your other options are and how a simple call works.
item.content:encoded:
"I just need to talk to someone."

Not a diagnosis. Not an intake form. Not a claim on your insurance or a call to the number on the back of your employer's benefits card. Just a calm human who will listen for a while and help you think straight again.

If that's where you are, you're not being dramatic and you're not avoiding anything. You're being specific about what you need. That's a good thing.

Why does starting therapy feel like such a big step?

Because it often is one. Therapy is real, valuable work, and for a lot of things (depression that won't lift, trauma, anxiety that runs your life, anything that needs a diagnosis) it's exactly the right call.

But it usually comes with a process. Finding someone in network. Waiting lists. Paperwork. A commitment to weekly sessions. Sometimes it goes through insurance, which means a record. Sometimes it goes through your employer's program, and even when that's confidential, it can feel a little close to work.

None of that is wrong. It's just a lot when what you need this week is to say the thing out loud to someone who won't flinch.

Is it okay to want to talk to someone without starting therapy?

Yes. Wanting to be heard is not a symptom. Humans have always talked things through with other humans: at kitchen tables, on porches, on long drives. Our nervous systems settle faster when another calm nervous system is nearby. That's called co-regulation, and you can read more about it in what co-regulation is.

The trouble is that a lot of us don't have that person right now. Friends are stretched thin. Family is complicated. Your partner is part of the thing you need to talk about. So the need doesn't go away. It just goes unmet.

What are my options if I just want to talk?

Here are the honest options, from free to paid:

  • A friend who can actually listen. Ask directly: "Do you have 20 minutes to just listen? I don't need advice."
  • A support group. Many are free and organized around a shared experience, like grief or caregiving.
  • A warmline. Some communities run free, non-crisis lines staffed by peers. Search "warmline" plus your state.
  • A crisis line, if you're not safe. That's what 988 is for. Use it.
  • An emotional support call. A short, paid conversation with a trained person. No insurance, no employer, nothing on your record.

That last one is what we do at The Emotional Support Line.

What happens on an emotional support call?

You pay, pick a time and we call you. It's 30 minutes with a calm, trained, real human. Never AI.

The call has a simple shape:

  1. You talk. About whatever is going on. Feelings are welcome. All of them.
  2. We help you settle. If your body is in fight-or-flight, we start there, because nobody makes good decisions with their heart pounding.
  3. We brainstorm. Once you're steadier, we look at the situation together and find one practical next step.

That's it. We're not going to make you talk about your mother for years. We're pragmatic: get regulated, get clear, take a step. For more detail, read what an emotional support call is.

Does an emotional support call go through insurance?

No. You pay directly, so nothing is billed to insurance, nothing goes through your employer's plan, and nothing lands on a medical record. It's not therapy, and our supporters aren't therapists. It's a conversation with a person who is trained to listen well and help you find your footing.

A call is $75. If you're a member of the Nest, it's $50, and every $75 call includes a free month in the Nest.

A quick check before you reach out

Not sure what you need yet? Try this. It takes two minutes.

  1. Name it. Finish this sentence: "The thing that's bothering me most is..."
  2. Rate it. On a scale of 1 to 10, how loud is it in your body right now?
  3. Choose. Do you need to be heard, to calm down, or to make a plan?

If you need to calm down first, start with the free 10-Minute Human Reset. If you need to be heard or to make a plan, that's what a call is for.

When is therapy the better fit?

If you've felt hopeless for weeks, can't function at work or at home, are dealing with trauma or addiction, or think you might need medication, please talk to your doctor or a licensed therapist. That's real care for a real need, and a support call isn't a replacement for it. Plenty of people use both.

And this isn't a crisis line. If you're in danger or thinking about suicide, call or text 988 (US).

Ready to talk it through?

You don't have to have the right words. You don't have to know what's wrong. You just have to pick a time.

Calls are Mondays and Tuesdays, noon to 7 pm Mountain. Book a support call, and a real person will call you.

item.title: Feeling stuck in life? Why it happens and what to do next
item.description: Feeling stuck in life usually isn't laziness or a lack of purpose. Here are the seven most common reasons people get stuck, and one small way to get unstuck for each.
item.content:encoded:
Feeling stuck in life is one of the most common things people tell us. Not in crisis. Not falling apart. Just... not moving. Same job, same arguments, same to-do list, same feeling that there should be more than this.

Here's the good news: stuck almost never means lazy. It usually means one of seven things.

Why do I feel stuck?

1. You're overwhelmed. When everything is urgent, nothing moves. Try: settle first. The 10-Minute Human Reset helps.

2. You're unclear. You don't know what you want, so every option feels flat. Try: ask "If no one would be disappointed, what would I do?"

3. You're afraid. You know the next step and it scares you. Try: name the smallest version of it you could take this week.

4. You're under-supported. You've been figuring it out alone for too long. Try: talk it through with someone neutral.

5. You're out of time. Every hour belongs to someone else. Try: write down yesterday hour by hour and circle one thing to drop.

6. Money is tight. Money worries can freeze everything else. Try: look at the feeling under the numbers before the numbers themselves.

7. You're disconnected from yourself. You've been who everyone needs for so long, you've forgotten who you are. Try: one hour this week that belongs only to you.

How to get unstuck

You don't need to find one grand purpose or fix your whole life today. You need one next step that you can actually take. Movement creates clarity, not the other way around.

Not sure which kind of stuck you are? Take the 2-minute quiz. You'll get your result and one thing to try today.

When stuck turns into something more

If you feel hopeless, can't get out of bed, or have stopped enjoying almost everything for weeks, please talk to your doctor or a licensed therapist. That's more than stuck, and you deserve real care. If you're thinking about suicide, call or text 988 (US).

item.title: How much does a life coach cost? (And other ways to get support)
item.description: Life coaches typically charge about $75 to $300 or more per session, and packages often run into the thousands. Here's what you get at each price, when coaching is worth it, and lower-cost ways to get support.
item.content:encoded:
Life coaching prices are all over the place, which makes it hard to know what's fair. Here's a plain guide.

How much does a life coach cost per session?

Industry guides put most life coaches somewhere in these ranges (Noomii, 2026):

  • Newer coaches: about $75 to $150 a session
  • Experienced coaches: about $150 to $300 an hour
  • Specialized or well-known coaches: $300 to $500 a session, and executive coaches can charge far more

Many coaches sell packages instead, and three-month packages often cost a few thousand dollars.

What affects the price?

Experience, specialty, how much access you get between sessions, and whether it's one-on-one or group. Higher price doesn't always mean a better fit. The best coach is the one you'll actually be honest with.

Is a life coach worth it?

Coaching is worth paying for when you have a clear goal, like a career change, a business or a big life decision, and you want structure and accountability for months. It's less useful when what you need right now is to be heard, or to calm down enough to think.

Cheaper ways to get support

  • A single support call. At The Emotional Support Line, a 30-minute call with a real person is $75, and comes with a free month in the Nest.
  • A membership. The Nest is $19 a month: Year of YES! courses with workbooks, guided meditations, a live group call every month, and $50 calls.
  • Group calls. Being in a room (or a video call) with other people working on the same things is powerful, and costs less than one-on-one.

And if you do want coaching

Year of YES! Coaching with Tracee Sioux is a 12-month program, two hours a month, guided by your Human Design chart, and it includes the Nest. It's by application, so you'll know it's a fit before you start.

item.title: I need someone to talk to: what are my options?
item.description: Need someone to talk to but you're not in crisis and don't want to start therapy? Here are your real options, from friends to a 30-minute call with a real person, and how to choose.
item.content:encoded:
"I need someone to talk to."

If you've typed that into a search bar, you're not alone, and nothing is wrong with you. Most of the time it doesn't mean an emergency. It means something is sitting on your chest, it's been going around in your head for too long, and you need to say it out loud to a person who will actually listen.

You don't have to be in crisis to need support. And not every hard day needs therapy. Sometimes you need someone to listen, help you sort through what you're feeling, and brainstorm what comes next.

Here are your options.

Can I talk to someone if I'm not in crisis?

Yes. Crisis lines exist for danger: if you're thinking about suicide or you're not safe, call or text 988 in the US right now. But most of what people carry isn't a crisis. It's a decision that won't settle, a relationship that's wearing you down, a week where everything is too much, or a loneliness that's hard to name.

That middle ground is real, and it deserves support too.

Your options, from free to paid

A friend, with a clear ask. Friends often want to help but don't know how. Make it easy: "I don't need advice. Can I talk for ten minutes?" The ask matters more than the friend.

Someone outside your life. Sometimes the people closest to you are part of the situation, or you don't want to burden them again. A neutral person has no stake in what you decide, which makes honesty much easier.

A support call. At The Emotional Support Line, you can book a 30-minute call with a calm, trained human. You talk, they listen, reflect back what they hear, and help you find one clear next step. No membership needed, no sales call first, and every call comes with a free month in the Nest. It's not therapy: no insurance, nothing through your employer, nothing on your record, and nobody making you talk about your childhood for years. Just a real person helping you get out of fight-or-flight and find a practical way forward.

A coach. If you want to change something over months, like a career, a habit or a direction, coaching gives you structure and accountability.

A therapist. If you're dealing with a mental health condition, trauma that keeps resurfacing, or symptoms that make daily life hard, a licensed therapist is the right fit. We'll always tell you if that's what we hear.

Who can I talk to when I don't want to burden my friends?

This is one of the most common reasons people reach out to us. You've already told your best friend three times. Your partner is tired of the topic. You're the strong one, and the strong one doesn't usually get to fall apart.

That's exactly what a neutral listener is for. You don't owe them anything afterward, and you don't have to manage their feelings about your problem.

What happens when you talk to someone?

Saying it out loud does something thinking can't. You hear where the story gets stuck. You notice what you're actually afraid of. Often, the next step shows up halfway through a sentence.

There's a body side to it too. Humans calm down with other humans. A steady voice on the other end of the line helps a wired nervous system settle, which is why talking often feels like relief before anything is solved. (That's called co-regulation.)

Not sure what kind of help you need?

Take the 2-minute "What do I need right now?" quiz, or read therapist vs life coach vs emotional support to see which fits.

And if you just need to talk it through, we're here.

item.title: Nervous system regulation in real life: a reset that doesn't have to be a solo project
item.description: What nervous system regulation actually means, what a dysregulated nervous system can feel like, what a "vagus nerve reset" can and can't do, and a free 10-minute reset you can use today.
item.content:encoded:
"Regulate your nervous system" is everywhere right now. So is "vagus nerve reset." Underneath the trend is something real and useful, and simpler than the internet makes it look.

What is nervous system regulation?

Your nervous system is constantly shifting between states: alert and ready to act, calm and connected, and sometimes shut down and numb. Regulation isn't about being calm all the time. It's about being able to come back to steady after something stirs you up.

A regulated day still has stress in it. You just don't stay stuck in it.

What can a dysregulated nervous system feel like?

Everyone's different, but common signs include:

  • Feeling wired and exhausted at the same time
  • Snapping at people, then feeling guilty
  • Racing thoughts, especially at night
  • Going numb, scrolling for hours, or not being able to start anything
  • Feeling like everything is urgent

These are common human responses to too much for too long, not a diagnosis. If symptoms are severe or not going away, talk to your doctor or a licensed professional.

What a "vagus nerve reset" can and can't do

The vagus nerve is part of how your body shifts into rest. Slow breathing with long exhales, humming, singing and gentle movement are simple ways many people find settling, and they're free.

What they can't do is fix the reason you keep getting overwhelmed. If your life has too much in it, or you're carrying something alone, a two-minute hack will help for two minutes. That's still worth something. It's just not the whole answer.

A nervous system reset that includes people

Most resets stop at breathing. Ours has one more step, because humans regulate with humans. The free 10-Minute Human Reset walks you through:

  1. Name it. Three words for what's going on inside.
  2. Breathe out longer than you breathe in. Ten slow rounds.
  3. Look around. Five things you can see, three you can hear.
  4. Feel your feet and your weight. Ground on the floor, or on the earth.
  5. Reach for a human. Text, call or talk to someone steady.

When to get support

If you've done every breathing exercise and still feel flooded, that's not failure. It might mean you need co-regulation: a calm person to talk it through with. Book a 30-minute call, or start with the 2-minute quiz to see what you need right now.

item.title: Therapist vs life coach vs emotional support: what kind of help do I need?
item.description: Life coach or therapist? Or do you just need someone to talk to? A plain-English guide to what each kind of help does, what it costs, and how to choose what fits right now.
item.content:encoded:
You know you need something. But what? A therapist? A life coach? A friend? A crisis line?

These are different jobs, and choosing the right one saves you time, money and a lot of frustration. Here's a plain-English guide.

The quick answer

I need... Consider
Diagnosis or treatment of a mental health condition A licensed therapist or your doctor
Help right now because I'm not safe A crisis line: call or text 988 (US) or 911
Structured change toward a goal over months A coach
Financial planning or investment advice A qualified financial professional
Someone to listen and help me think something through Emotional support, like The Emotional Support Line
Help settling down and sorting out what I need next Emotional support
Ongoing human support plus personal growth tools A membership like the Nest

What does a therapist do?

A therapist is a licensed mental health professional. Therapy is the right choice when you're dealing with depression, anxiety that disrupts daily life, trauma, addiction, or anything that needs assessment and treatment. Therapists can diagnose, and they're trained for deep, long-term work. Insurance sometimes covers it, and there are often waiting lists.

What does a life coach do?

A life coach helps you move toward a goal: a career change, a business, a habit, a big decision. Coaching looks forward. It's structured, usually runs for weeks or months, and is about action and accountability. Coaches don't diagnose or treat. Prices vary widely, from around $75 to $300 or more a session (see how much a life coach costs).

What is emotional support?

Emotional support is the human kind of help most of us actually need most often: someone calm who listens, reflects back what they hear, and helps you find your footing. It's for the in-between, when nothing is catastrophically wrong, but you need to talk it through.

At The Emotional Support Line, that looks like a 30-minute call: one issue, one real person, one clear next step. It's not therapy, and it's not a crisis line. It's talking about feelings, brainstorming solutions and settling your nervous system, with a person.

How is emotional support different from therapy?

We're not therapy, on purpose:

  • We don't touch your insurance or your employer's plan. No diagnosis, no claim, nothing on your record.
  • We won't make you talk about your mother for years. The past matters, but you don't have to excavate it to feel better this week.
  • We're pragmatic. First we help you get out of fight-or-flight, because nobody thinks clearly while their alarm is going off. Then we co-regulate: humans calm down with humans, and if you don't have people in your life for that right now, that's what we're here for. Then we brainstorm a practical next step you can take with a steadier nervous system.

Therapy is the right fit for diagnosing and treating mental health conditions and for deep trauma work. If what we hear sounds like it needs that, we'll tell you.

Is a life coach worth it? Is therapy worth it?

Both are worth it when they fit the job. Coaching is worth paying for when you have a clear goal and need structure. Therapy is worth it when something is affecting your health or your ability to function.

Neither is a great fit when what you really need is to be heard this week. That's where a single support call often does more, for a lot less.

Can I use more than one?

Yes, and many people do. Some of our callers see a therapist monthly and call us between sessions when something comes up. Some work with a coach and use a call to untangle the feelings that keep getting in the way of the plan.

Still not sure?

Take the 2-minute "What do I need right now?" quiz. Six questions, and you'll get a plain answer and one thing to try today.

item.title: What is co-regulation? Why humans calm down with humans
item.description: Co-regulation is how one calm nervous system helps another settle. It's not just for babies. Here's what co-regulation between adults looks like, and how to get more of it.
item.content:encoded:
You've probably felt it. You're spinning, you call the right person, and five minutes into the conversation your shoulders drop. Nothing has been solved yet. But you can breathe again.

That's co-regulation.

What is co-regulation?

Co-regulation is the way one person's settled nervous system helps another person's settle. It happens through tone of voice, pace, facial expression and simply feeling that someone is with you.

It's how babies learn to calm down: a parent's steady presence does the regulating before the child can do it alone. But we never outgrow it. Adults co-regulate all day long, with partners, friends, colleagues and, yes, sometimes their dogs.

Co-regulation vs self-regulation

Most nervous system advice is about self-regulation: breathing, humming, cold water, shaking it out, getting your feet on the grass. Those tools are useful, and we teach several of them in the free 10-Minute Human Reset.

But if you only ever try to calm down alone, you're doing it the hard way. Humans are social animals. A lot of us learned to "handle it ourselves" because there wasn't anyone steady around, and that can leave you feeling like regulation is another job you're failing at.

It doesn't have to be a solo project. Sometimes another nervous system is the intervention.

What does co-regulation between adults look like?

  • A friend who listens without rushing to fix it
  • A partner who sits beside you without talking
  • A slow, steady voice on the other end of a phone call
  • Walking side by side with someone, instead of facing them
  • Laughing together, which is a surprisingly fast reset

Signs you need co-regulation, not another technique

  • You've tried the breathing exercises and you're still wired
  • You keep replaying the same conversation in your head
  • You feel calmer the moment you're around certain people
  • You've been "fine" alone for a long time, and you're tired

How to get more co-regulation in your life

Ask for presence, not advice. "Can you just stay on the phone with me while I walk?" is a complete request.

Notice your calm people. Who leaves you more settled than they found you? Spend more time near them.

Use a neutral person. If the people closest to you are part of what's stressing you, talking to someone outside your life can be easier. That's what our 30-minute calls are for: a calm, real person who listens, so you can settle and think.

We call it talking about feelings, brainstorming solutions and regulating nervous systems. Together.

item.description: Worried AI will change your job, or already living it? Here's how to find out who you are beyond your title, using Human Design and a year of saying YES! to your real gifts.
item.content:encoded:
Work is changing fast. Every week there's another headline about AI doing jobs people trained for years to do. Maybe you're watching it happen at your company. Maybe you're quietly wondering, "If my job changes or disappears, who am I?"

That's the real question. Not "what will I do for money?" (that matters, and we'll get to practical next steps). The deeper one: who are you when the title is gone?

Is your identity your job?

For a lot of us, the honest answer is yes. We were raised to pick a major, get the degree (and the debt), land the corporate gig, and climb. Somewhere along the way, "what do you do?" became "who are you?"

But your job was never the reason you're here. The Universe didn't put you here, right now, so you could update spreadsheets until retirement. You have gifts and talents that no machine can copy, because they're wired into how you are built.

Stop being who you were conditioned to be

Most of us spent decades becoming who society told us to be: agreeable, productive, busy, small enough to fit. That conditioning got us through school and into jobs. It doesn't tell us who we are.

Human Design is one of the most useful tools we know for getting underneath it. Your chart, based on your birth date, time and place, shows how you're designed to make decisions, where your energy naturally flows, and what you're here to do. Learn who you are. Explore it. Then stop apologizing for it, and BE who you are.

You can get your free Human Design chart in about a minute.

What do you do when work is uncertain?

Fear makes people grab the nearest safe-looking option, and it's usually a smaller version of the old life. Before you react:

  1. Get out of fight-or-flight first. Nobody makes a good career decision with their alarm going off. Try the free 10-Minute Human Reset.
  2. Write down what people always come to you for. Not your job duties. The thing friends call you about. That's a clue to your gifts.

  4. Talk it through with a real person. Saying the scary part out loud, "I don't know who I am if I'm not this," is often where the breakthrough starts. Book a 30-minute call.

item.title: Why can't I get anything done? Maybe it's not a motivation problem
item.description: Can't get anything done no matter how many productivity tips you try? It might not be motivation. Here's how to tell whether you have an information, emotion or capacity problem, and what to do about each.
item.content:encoded:
You've read the productivity books. You've tried the apps, the planners, the 5 am routine. And you still can't get anything done.

Here's a different question: what if it's not a motivation problem at all?

Three reasons you're not getting things done

1. An information problem. You don't actually know the next step. The task is "sort out the finances" instead of "find last month's bank statement." Fix: break it down until the first step takes less than ten minutes.

2. An emotion problem. You know the step, but it brings up something: fear of failing, dread of a conversation, shame about how long it's taken. Your brain avoids the feeling by avoiding the task. Fix: name the feeling out loud. Talking it through with someone often unlocks it faster than any app.

3. A capacity problem. You're overloaded. Your nervous system is running on empty, and every task feels like a mountain. Fix: don't start with productivity. Start by settling. Try the 10-Minute Human Reset, then pick one thing.

Signs you're overloaded, not lazy

  • You're tired and wired at the same time
  • Small tasks feel huge
  • You spend the day busy and finish with nothing done
  • You feel guilty resting, so you don't really rest

What actually helps

Less, not more. Drop, delegate or do half as well one thing this week.

White Space. Unscheduled time is not wasted time. It's where your capacity comes back.

Someone to think out loud with. A lot of "procrastination" dissolves once you've said the scary part to another person.

The Time Joy-gasm course in the Nest is ten short classes on exactly this: true values first, energy levels, phone rules, delegating and more.
